To lollop means to move with big, loose, bouncy, and clumsy movements. It's the kind of motion where the body seems to flop and roll along rather than move in a smooth, controlled way. Imagine a large, excited dog bounding toward you — its body bouncing up and down, its limbs moving a little too freely, its ears flopping with every stride. That dog is lolloping.
Breaking Down What the Movement Actually Looks Like

To truly understand lollop, picture all these qualities happening together:

1. Bounding and bouncy
There is a distinct rise and fall to the movement — the person or animal seems to leap and land repeatedly, with a lot of up-and-down motion. It's not flat and smooth like a sprint. It's almost like galloping, but less controlled.

2. Loose and floppy
The limbs, body parts, ears, or fur move freely and loosely rather than staying tight and disciplined. Things are jiggling and swinging. There's a general sense of "too much movement" happening.

3. Heavy and ungainly
It's not a light, nimble movement. There's a certain weightiness or clumsiness to it. The creature isn't gliding — it's thumping and flopping along.

4. Energetic but not graceful
Lolloping is not slow or lazy. There is momentum and energy. But that energy hasn't been refined into elegance. Think of a puppy that runs fast but has no idea what its own legs are doing.

The word is most naturally and most often used for animals, especially large ones with loose bodies:

  • Big dogs — a Labrador, a golden retriever, a greyhound
  • Rabbits — the way they bound and hop in an uneven, loopy way
  • Bears — their rolling, lumbering run has a lolloping quality
  • Horses — at a loose canter, sometimes described as lolloping
  • Large birds running on the ground

It can also be used for people, usually affectionately or humorously — a tall teenager with long limbs, an overexcited child, someone running awkwardly but happily.
The Tone and Feeling of the Word

This is important: lollop is not an insult. When you use it, you are not being cruel about someone's clumsiness. The word carries a warm, slightly amused, even affectionate tone. It suggests endearing clumsiness — the kind you find charming rather than embarrassing.

If you say someone "stumbled clumsily," that sounds negative. If you say they "lolloped," it sounds almost lovable. There is something cheerful and exuberant buried in the word. The creature lolloping is usually doing so with abandon, without self-consciousness, with joy.

• "The golden retriever lolloped across the beach, tongue hanging out."
  • "A young rabbit lolloped through the garden and disappeared under the hedge."
  • "The bear lolloped along the riverbank, swaying from side to side."
  • "She watched her son lollop down the stairs two at a time, nearly tumbling at the bottom."
  • "The foal lolloped awkwardly across the field, still getting used to its own legs."
How It Differs from Similar Words

A few comparisons will sharpen your understanding:

  • Lumber / lumber along — slow, heavy, and plodding. A lumbering creature is not fast. A lolloping creature has energy and speed.
  • Gallop — fast and powerful, but controlled and rhythmic. Lolloping suggests the coordination is missing.
  • Waddle — side-to-side movement (like a duck or penguin), slow and short-stepped. Lolloping is forward-bounding, not sideways-rocking.
  • Amble — easy, relaxed, and casual walking. No bouncing or flopping involved.
  • Bound — to bound is similar, but "bound" sounds more athletic and intentional. Lolloping sounds looser and funnier.

So: lollop sits in its own space — it is faster than a waddle, looser than a gallop, and warmer and funnier than any of them.
A Mental Image to Lock It In

Picture a large, happy Labrador who has just spotted its owner at the other end of a park. It takes off running — but it's so excited that its back legs nearly overtake its front legs, its body rolls, its ears flap, its tongue swings wildly. It's not the most dignified run you've ever seen. But it's full of life. It arrives in a joyful, sprawling heap.

That is lolloping.

Whenever you need to describe movement that is bounding, loose, heavy, clumsy, and yet somehow full of cheerful energy — lollop is your word.
